cards.html: Volume, range and sum catch broken data. The errors that fool smart people come from data that is perfectly clean and still lying. Two patterns cause most of them: an average that moved because the mix changed, and a correlation that looks like a cause.

cards.s: Trap 1: the mix changed, not the thing
cards.html: In June, Parla's activation rate (the share of brand-new users who did something meaningful, like completing three lessons, in their first 7 days) fell from 30% to 24%. It looked like the product got worse. It had not. On June 1 marketing had launched a new TikTok ad channel, and TikTok brought a flood of lower-intent browsers. Every existing sign-up source held steady at its old rate. The company average dropped only because the mix of sources shifted toward the new, lower-converting one. This is a mix shift.

cards.s: Trap 1: the mix changed, not the thing
cards.html:
A small worked version, with two sources:

SourceRate beforeShare beforeRate afterShare after
Existing sources33%85%33%50%
TikTok13%15%15%50%

Before: 0.85 × 33% + 0.15 × 13% = 28.05% + 1.95% = 30%. After: 0.5 × 33% + 0.5 × 15% = 16.5% + 7.5% = 24%. TikTok even improved a little, existing sources held, and the total still fell 6 points.

When a mix shift flips the direction of the headline, it is called Simpson's paradox: every group improves (or holds), yet the total moves the other way, because the group sizes changed. Parla's satisfaction score did exactly this from one quarter to the next: it fell overall, even though both free users and Plus members individually got happier, because the user base tilted toward lower-scoring free users.

The fix is a reflex: before you explain a moved average, break it out by segment. If the segments did not move but the total did, your story is about the mix, not the product.

cards.s: Trap 2: correlation that looks like cause
cards.html: Learners who use Word Bank buy Plus at about three times the rate of those who do not. That looks like a giant lever: push everyone to save words and triple your sales. But when Parla ran a proper randomised test (August 1 to September 30; half of learners shown Word Bank more prominently, half not), the real lift (the gain the feature actually caused) was small: 16.5% of the test group bought Plus versus 15.3% of the control. A difference of just over one point, only about 8% higher than the control's rate.

cards.s: Trap 2: correlation that looks like cause
cards.html: The 3× was almost entirely because high-intent learners, the ones already likely to buy, are also the ones who bother saving words. The button did not cause the buying; the intent caused both. Ask of any impressive gap: could a third thing be driving both sides? If the only evidence is that two things move together, the honest recommendation is "run a test", not "ship it everywhere".

A confound is an outside factor that could be the real cause of a result: a promotion, a holiday, an outage, a launch running at the same time. The Black Friday sale on top of the Android payment redesign (skill 7) is one. Keep the promotion and launch calendar next to any metric you report, and check it before you claim credit.
